title: Building ambitious software — Jonathan Kelley, Dioxus Labs & Cognition
talk_summary: Jonathan Kelley of Dioxus Labs describes how a 3-engineer team adopted coding agents for a large Rust framework, finding agents excel at knowledge-heavy debugging, mundane release chores, and test harnesses, but produce slop when architecture and intent aren't controlled. Their core lesson: code is cheap now but quality is not, so human effort shifts to architecture, line-by-line PR review, and intent communication.

takeaways.technique: Human line-by-line review on top of AI review, gated by intent quality
takeaways.what_they_do: They run AI review to spot bugs ahead of time but still read every PR line by line, because contributors (and agents) often don't communicate intent and glue solutions in place.

takeaways.technique: Architecture-first work supply; agents don't self-refactor
takeaways.what_they_do: They observe agents won't voluntarily do a big refactor or redesign when a feature doesn't fit; they just ship. So the team spends most development time on architecture and future evolution, and treats that as the scarce input.
takeaways.evidence_quote: coding agents aren't typically afraid to voluntarily go on a huge refactor of a system or redesign the architecture when a feature doesn't quite fit. They'll typically just ship.

takeaways.technique: Agents build test harnesses and fuzzers, humans enumerate test conditions
takeaways.what_they_do: They found agents write sloppy tests (test the constructor you gave them) and fail to pick the right tests, but are excellent at building fuzzing/test harnesses and as a sounding board for edge cases; humans still enumerate conditions and craft test APIs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: one place that we have actually really enjoyed using coding agents to do testing is building test harnesses. So, fuzzing is a critical part

takeaways.technique: Route mundane verification chores to agents to free scarce human/planner attention
takeaways.what_they_do: They hand agents tedious, repetitive checks (tarball extracts to right dir, editor extension still works, release checklists, backporting, doc/comment freshness) so engineers spend time on architecture.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Applying agents to the problem actually lets us automate many of these like hard tedious tasks that would have taken like countless hours before.
takeaways.numbers: Shipped more patch releases in the most recent version than ever before; weekly or multiple-times-a-week cadence.

takeaways.technique: Intent/context in the prompt is the quality lever
takeaways.what_they_do: They stress that implementation quality depends heavily on the prompt and on communicating intent; agents can't read minds, so unclear intent yields glued-in solutions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: as ridiculous as it sounds, prompt engineering is quite real. The quality of an implementation can be very much dependent on the the prompt that you give the model

takeaways.technique: Point agents at authoritative sources (specs, upstream source) instead of pre-digesting
takeaways.what_they_do: Agents excel at sifting thousands of pages of docs, reading bespoke APIs, and recalling how Chrome/Safari handle CSS, so the team lets them dig into primary sources rather than hand-feeding summaries.
takeaways.evidence_quote: They can quickly quickly sift through thousands of pages of documentation, read all the bespoke APIs, dig into binaries, reverse engineer APIs.
